The post Reflections from Labour Party conference 2026 appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was authored by Rose Stephenson, Director of Policy and Strategy at the Higher Education Policy Institute.

HEPI is determinedly a non-partisan think tank and, as such, attends as many party conferences as our capacity allows. You can read a roundup from the Reform UK party conference from HEPI’s CEO, Nick Hillman, here and find out about our events at the Conservative Party conference here.

There is always an interesting discussion in the HEPI office about which party conferences we will attend and which ones we will run events at. The determining factors depend upon the electoral cycle. For the first two to three years of a parliament, our decision is weighed against the number of MPs in parliament. In the later stages of parliament, both the number of MPs and polling figures are taken into account. At this midpoint in the current parliament, this means attending both Labour and the official opposition Tory party conferences, as well as a sojourn by Nick to the Reform Party conference, given that at the time of our discussions they were the highest polling party in the UK.

And so, to Liverpool. This is the third Labour Party conference since they came to power, but the first for the new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham. There was certainly some strong messaging in action, with electronic billboards everywhere bearing the words ‘hope again’. But was there any hope of some focus on the higher education system?

Many, many NEETS (and occasionally some PEETS)

There were an impressive 17 events on NEETS at this year’s conference. This included a focus from our own sector, with the new Research+ (a new collaboration of research-intensive universities) hosting a panel on how to progress NEETS (those ‘not in employment, education or training’) to PEETS (who are ‘preparing for employment, education and training’). Across these events, themes such as mental health, neurodiversity, social capital (or lack thereof) and confidence were raised repeatedly. With Alan Millburn’s interim report stating that 21% of NEETs have a Level 3 (equivalent to A-level) qualification, and 15% have a university degree, the higher education system clearly has a place in solving this current crisis.

And that leads us on to …

Employment is everything

There is a clear drive across many institutions to focus on the employment of their students. And I am purposefully using the term employment rather than employability. Employability is helping the students to go out and develop their skills, but providers are now increasingly focussing beyond this – on employment itself. Many providers were discussing their programmes for providing work-based learning (including the University of Leicester, who held an early morning roundtable event on their new report with the Graduate Futures Institute). Others talked about a data-driven approach to graduate employment. Tracking those who were un- or underemployed after graduation and offering them internships at their own institutions or supported traineeships at local employers.

With a government that continues to focus on growth (now in every postcode), youth inactivity and intergenerational unfairness, this work feels on the money.

What else was being discussed?

Localism was big. Devolution is being supercharged by the Burnham government, and there was much discussion about working with mayoral combined authorities, and some helpful discussion about how institutions that sit outside of MCAs can act together to support funding being invested into these devolution cold spots until the devolution map is fully coloured in.

Vocational courses are in vogue. Perhaps inspired by governmental interest in vocational and technical education as an ‘alternative’ pathway to going to university.

VCs, including Penny Haughan of Liverpool Hope University, brought many of these themes together, talking proudly about their local student intake (57% are from the North West, 37% are from the City of Liverpool), their role in training teachers and social workers and the cyclical positive impact this has on the city and the region. As well as aligning with the messaging on youth employment, local focus and vocational learning, this institution has ‘hope’ in the name – how is that for supporting the agenda of the day?

We also ran an event about ‘soft power’, with Dr Naimat Zafary reminding us that international students are more than immigration numbers, tuition income figures or potential future monarchs. They’re students and humans and fathers and cricket players and dreamers of a better future who make a deep and lasting impact on the communities they join in the UK.

The elephant in the room?

At several higher education events, it felt that something was being unsaid. The issue of poor-quality provision was barely mentioned, including by the Minister for Skills at an evening reception. (Although I did enjoy Baroness Smith’s description of the higher education sector as ‘not unargumentative’ and her recognition of how helpful the ‘constructive tension’ between higher education and the Government could be).

Sometimes, the most interesting talking points come from those listening to events. We hoped to capture this with our ‘Vice-Chancellor Question Time’ event, and it did not disappoint. One audience member asked a barnstormer of a question: if the Government is so concerned about the quality of franchised provision, is transnational education (UK institutions delivering courses abroad) going to be the next scandal?

And so – onto Birmingham for the Conservative Party Conference. HEPI will be running a panel event on Soft Power and Vice-Chancellor Question Time will be making a comeback; so if you do have a spicy question to ask – get yourself there, we’re outside the secure zone so no pass required.

With huge thanks to our partners and sponsors for the Liverpool Party Conference events: Duolingo, the University of Leicester, Royal Holloway, University of London Liverpool Hope University, Cambridge University Press and Assessment, the University of the Arts, London and the University of Manchester. We could not put on these events without your support.

title: MI5 warns UK universities over ‘theft of tech secrets by Chinese front company’
summary:
Security service says academics should stop working with and taking grants from firm backed by Chinese intelligence

  • MI5 China alert will send chill through UK’s cash-strapped universities

MI5 has issued a rare public warning to UK universities that China’s intelligence service is using a front company to pay for research by UK academics and steal the secrets of hi-tech projects.

Britain’s domestic security service said researchers and academics should cease work with the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI), sometimes also known as the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT).

Additional reporting by Helena Horton

Continue reading...
full_text:
MI5 has issued a rare public warning to UK universities that China’s intelligence service is using a front company to pay for research by UK academics and steal the secrets of hi-tech projects.

Britain’s domestic security service said researchers and academics should cease work with the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI), sometimes also known as the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT).

MI5 believes the body poses a “significant threat” and is now prepared to say publicly that the CGTRI is a front for Chinese intelligence, namely the Chinese ministry of state security (MSS). It said continued collaboration by UK academics could be prosecuted under the National Security Act 2023.

The Chinese organisation has funded 100 or more academics at a string of universities across the UK, in return for access to the research, which it is alleged found its way back to China’s intelligence service.

On Wednesday, the Chinese embassy in London issued a strongly worded rebuttal, describing the accusations as “imaginary and purely fabricated”. A spokesperson said: “We firmly oppose such baseless allegations and have lodged solemn representations with the UK side.

“Exchanges and collaboration between UK universities and China have always been conducted on a voluntary basis and in compliance with laws and regulations. Such exchanges and collaboration are mutually beneficial.”

The MI5 warning sent a shock wave through the UK university sector, with staff reviewing the implications for existing or future partnerships with China, and experts raising concerns about the rigour of the vetting process in sensitive research collaborations.

Areas of research targeted include AI, cybersecurity, covert communications and steganography – the embedding of secret data in seemingly innocuous files. MI5 believes it has clear evidence of sensitive information being passed back to Chinese intelligence, and the Guardian understands that some British-based academics were given honours and awards by the Chinese as well as research money.

Successive British governments have courted Chinese investment and encouraged academic cooperation. Sam Dunning, the director of the UK-China Transparency group, said: “It is reasonably obvious from the internet that CGTRI was focused on areas of high interest to the military and intelligence services.

“Granted, CGTRI used various aliases and have certainly obscured some funding streams, but as for the UK universities or academics who knew they were dealing with CGTRI, open-source research made clear that CGTRI had military or intelligence links.”

Vice-chancellors who spoke to the Guardian said they were not aware of receiving any funding from the Chinese institute, but warned that individual academics working on joint projects with other universities or third parties may not know the original sources of funding.

Prof Peter Mathieson, vice-chancellor of the University of Edinburgh and the lead for international security for Universities UK, which represents 142 institutions across the UK, said MI5’s warning meant that future collaborations with the CGTRI would be illegal.

“They are saying that anyone who has a link to this institute up until now has not committed any kind of offence, because it’s not previously been said this was a high-risk activity.

“Now that they have said it, we have to sit up and take notice. It’s very much a forward-looking directive.

He added: “I can’t speak for MI5, but I think what they are attempting to say is that people may not realise that the institute they are working with is connected to the security services of the Beijing government. And there’s no reason why anyone should have realised that, because it’s a new piece of information that MI5 has discovered.”

In the alert issued on Wednesday, the Security Service said: “MI5 has identified that the primary purpose of CGTRI is to fund academic research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage.”

It said that CGTRI had “very strong ties to the … MSS, China’s civilian intelligence and security service”.

The alert continued: “Many academic institutions and individuals will to date have engaged with CGTRI in good faith given CGTRI’s obfuscated links to MSS.

“UK academic institutions are strongly advised to immediately review any ongoing or planned collaboration with CGTRI. This is to ensure MSS derives no further benefit from UK universities or research institutions. Further, academics are advised to establish the ultimate funding source when conducting any research collaboration with Chinese institutions, to ensure CGTRI is not involved.”

That MI5 has decided on a public alert as a deterrence strategy, rather than trying to pursue every single case, demonstrates the scale of Chinese state espionage targeting the UK. It hopes universities will heed the warning and immediately cease their work with CGTRI.

The Guardian understands that cutting-edge British research on scraping social media (gathering large amounts of information from social sites and apps) is among the data to which MI5 believes Chinese intelligence gained access.

The security minister, Dan Jarvis, demanded universities end ties to the CGTRI. He said: “This alert exposes attempts by Chinese intelligence to covertly benefit from the expertise and research of our academics, undermining our national security and that of our allies.

“I have written to all university vice-chancellors to ensure they support their staff to end all arrangements with this company, preventing further benefit to the Chinese intelligence services and ensuring compliance with the National Security Act.”

Responding to the MI5 alert, Vivienne Stern, the chief executive of Universities UK, said universities took their responsibilities around research security and national security extremely seriously.

“The sector has made significant investments in recent years to strengthen due diligence, risk assessment and research security processes, while continuing to support the international collaboration that is essential to world-leading research and innovation,” she said.

Chinese government filings suggest that CAGT is connected to the China General Technology Group, a major state-owned conglomerate administered directly by the government of China that is also known as Genertec.

The Genertec brand has a UK presence, with a company called Genertec (UK) Ltd, appearing to be owned by the Chinese state.

The British company, which has been registered in the UK for a decade and is based in a shared office address on Southwark Bridge Road, had £5.6m in the bank according to accounts to the end of 2024 – cash that seems to have come exclusively from a single property transaction.

title: The Guardian view on falling pupil numbers: a chance to improve opportunities for young people | Editorial
summary:
Empty classrooms are a sign of falling fertility and high living costs. But they should also free up more resources to spend on young people

School closures are an alarming symptom of Britain’s shrinking birthrate. Several factors have contributed to falling enrolment, but the most significant is that people are having fewer children. Declining pupil numbers could be an excuse to free up spending for an ageing population. Instead, the government should see this as an opportunity to improve the quality of provision for young people.

The fall has been most acute in inner London, where 90 schools have shut since 2021. In Southwark, where the number of children born each year has dropped by more than a third since 2010, eight primary schools have closed in the past six years. As London’s councils have observed, high living costs are pricing families out of the centre and dissuading people from having children. It is no surprise that Islington and Westminster, two of the most expensive places to live in Britain, also have among the lowest fertility rates in England and Wales.

full_text:
School closures are an alarming symptom of Britain’s shrinking birthrate. Several factors have contributed to falling enrolment, but the most significant is that people are having fewer children. Declining pupil numbers could be an excuse to free up spending for an ageing population. Instead, the government should see this as an opportunity to improve the quality of provision for young people.

The fall has been most acute in inner London, where 90 schools have shut since 2021. In Southwark, where the number of children born each year has dropped by more than a third since 2010, eight primary schools have closed in the past six years. As London’s councils have observed, high living costs are pricing families out of the centre and dissuading people from having children. It is no surprise that Islington and Westminster, two of the most expensive places to live in Britain, also have among the lowest fertility rates in England and Wales.

Declining enrolment shapes the quality of education that schools can provide. They receive funding for each child they enrol, which is currently £7,000 per primary-age pupil in England. Schools with fewer pupils are forced to make their funding stretch further, cutting teachers, merging classes, and losing extracurricular activities. Official forecasts have previously overestimated the future number of young people, making it harder for local authorities to plan. They have not been helped by the promotion of free schools, which have created a surplus of school places, or the expansion of academies, which decide their own admissions and can entice pupils away to neighbouring areas. The government has recently given local authorities greater powers to object to academy expansion, which should help them plan more effectively.

The Treasury may be tempted to recycle savings from falling pupil numbers towards rising demand for health and social care. Over the past seven years, for example, as primary school pupil numbers in England fell by 5%, the number of teachers and classes shrank by 4%. But treating this development as a justification for cutting spending on education would be a mistake. Lucy Powell, the education secretary, has promised expanded enrichment activities and earlier intervention for children with special educational needs. Falling pupil numbers offer an opportunity to deliver these ambitions, provided the government retains the resources to do so. The gap between private school fees and state school spending per pupil has more than doubled over the past decade, and spending more on state school pupils would help narrow this inequality.

The closure of a school shapes an area. “Without this school it’s all just tourists, isn’t it?” one parent recently said of Soho’s last remaining primary school, which is at risk of imminent closure. Fewer schools make areas less attractive to families, particularly in rural places where alternatives may be miles away. Yet if people continue having fewer children, more schools will probably have to close. In some cases, this may be unavoidable.

Schools that have large numbers of unfilled places tend to perform worse on average, but closing them won’t necessarily improve results. Local authorities, which have excelled at selling off public assets, should be required to keep hold of shuttered schools. Empty classrooms could be repurposed as youth clubs, turned over to nurseries, or transformed into Sure Start centres. The focus should be on managing resources to improve education and opportunities for young people in an increasingly old society.

title: ‘Voices against electoral 'capture' getting louder': Congress targets EC over SIR
full_text:
Congress stages protest against CEC in Ahmedabad

NEW DELHI: The Congress on Thursday said the “chorus of voices” against what it called the “capture of the electoral system” was growing louder, and asserted that citizens would no longer tolerate “vote chori” in any form. Congress general secretary in-charge communications Jairam Ramesh made the remarks while citing former chief election commissioner O P Rawat’s criticism of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Ramesh alleged that nearly 14 crore voters had already been disenfranchised through the exercise. “In an interview to a leading national daily, Former CEC O.P. Rawat has questioned the SIR and the violations committed by the ECI. It is ‘the first time since Independence that so many eligible voters have lost their vote’,” Ramesh said in a post on X. He further cited Rawat as saying that the Election Commission, once considered the “gold standard”, had lost credibility and that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi should have done more to oppose decisions they disagreed with.

INDIA bloc announces protests The Congress's latest attack came a day after the INDIA bloc announced a joint campaign against what opposition parties have described as irregularities in the electoral process. At a meeting attended by leaders of 19 opposition parties, the bloc announced joint “Save Democracy” marches across districts and five major rallies. Opposition MPs are also scheduled to march to the Election Commission on October 6, while opposition leaders plan to meet the President over alleged irregularities in voter-list revision. The bloc has also demanded that future elections be conducted using ballot papers and called for the Supreme Court to expedite cases concerning SIR and alleged electoral malpractices. The controversy comes as the Election Commission continues to review several issues linked to voter registration, electoral-roll databases and its IT systems following concerns raised internally by Sandhu and Joshi.

title: Finding the Right Disaster Recovery Strategy for Higher Ed
summary:
As higher education institutions prepare for unexpected events, from cyberattacks to unplanned downtime, disaster recovery is becoming a critical part of their survival. Having reliable, immutable backups is no longer just a matter of IT hygiene, it’s table stakes for operational continuity.
Though colleges and universities understand the importance of a strong disaster recovery strategy, they’re also concerned about costs and available skills among their lean teams. A Veeam survey found that 92% of IT professionals want backup solutions better tailored to their organizational needs.…
full_text:
How Higher Ed Can Rethink Their Approach to Disaster Recovery

Simply asking whether an institution has a backup solution is old-school thinking that needs to be retired. Chris Bevil, principal for global cyber resilience and artificial intelligence at Commvault, suggests reframing the question as, “Can I recover the parts of my organization that matter most, quickly and safely?” Recoverability, he says, is what determines whether an organization can survive a cyber incident.

Higher education institutions can start by identifying their most critical systems, such as payroll, billing, student data or email, Bevil notes, and define how long they can afford to be down and how much data they can afford to lose. “At the end of the day, having a copy of your data doesn’t help if you can’t cleanly restore it when it counts,” he adds.

Is Disaster Recovery as a Service a Good Fit?

Vanover says there are solutions that incorporate automation and managed recovery at a lower cost. A skills gap can be an issue among the smaller IT teams colleges may have, so relying on an on-demand service for disaster recovery may make more sense.

Bevil adds that institutions should evaluate a solution as “part of a broader operational continuity strategy, not just another cloud service.” He suggests these practical questions:

What systems need to recover first?

How fast do they need to come back?

Who actually declares a disaster?

Who is responsible for failover and failback?

How often is recovery tested and proven?

What costs show up during a real recovery event?

DISCOVER: Managed cyber resilience and disaster recovery services keep operations moving.

“DRaaS tends to make the most sense when an organization needs predictable, repeatable recovery but lacks the internal resources to build and maintain that capability itself. The simplest way to look at it: If you can’t confidently ensure recovery in-house, DRaaS should absolutely be on the table,” Bevil says.

The Role of Immutable Backups for Higher Ed

In this era, immutable backups are a must-have, Vanover says. If an institution doesn’t have one or more copies of its backup data that are immutable, that should be considered an emergency for its environment. In ransomware cases, where malicious actors can target backup data, having immutable storage is one of the most effective ways to support recovery.

Vanover says that the most ideal, “ultraresilient” storage has one or more of these characteristics: It’s offline, air-gapped, immutable or it requires at least two-person authorization. He also highlights the 3-2-1 backup rule: three (or more) copies of data on two different media, one of which is offsite.

Bevil agrees that immutable backups are becoming a baseline requirement for institutions, but they’re not something that can just be turned on and forgotten. Institutions should follow these guidelines:

Set the right retention windows

Lock down access controls

Enforce multifactor authentication

Regularly test restores

“Immutability isn’t a silver bullet. It won’t stop ransomware from getting in. But it significantly improves your ability to recover without paying an attacker. That’s the difference that matters,” Bevil says.

UP NEXT: Cybersecurity solutions lead to institutional resilience.

Prioritizing Backup and Recovery Amid Tight Budgets

People are as integral to disaster recovery as technology and processes. So, Vanover says, higher education institutions should consider cross-training their staff so that expertise and responsibility don’t fall to just one person on the team. If that expert is on vacation when downtime happens, there should be someone else who is trained and can step in. That could be a partner on retainer, he adds.

Bevil notes that organizations should not protect their entire environment at the same level, because that can lead to overspending in some areas while underprotecting the most critical systems.

The institutions best suited to recover aren’t always the ones with the biggest budgets, he adds: “They’re the ones that understand what matters most and have proved that they can get it back.”

title: The technical turn and what it means for higher education
summary: by Tim Savage When I began my career as a photography technician in higher education 25 years ago, the distinction between academic and technical work was clear and helpful. Academics were thought of as the ‘master practitioners’ who taught creative … Continue reading →
full_text:
by Tim Savage

When I began my career as a photography technician in higher education 25 years ago, the distinction between academic and technical work was clear and helpful. Academics were thought of as the ‘master practitioners’ who taught creative and professional practice, while technicians prepared facilities, maintained equipment, and helped students to use specialist resources safely. However, as my career progressed, I observed the boundaries between academic and technical roles and responsibilities becoming increasingly indistinct and porous.

In my most recent role, as Director of Technical Learning at a leading UK arts university, I led a technical team of 130 staff whose remits became deeply involved in teaching and learning; many gained teaching qualifications and sought professional recognition, and it became increasingly common for technicians to transition their careers into academia, particularly in disciplines driven by new and emerging technologies.

Technical duties at my institution evolved informally to include writing and delivering progressively developmental lesson plans aligned to module outcomes, devising innovative and differentiated ways of teaching advanced disciplinary skills, collaborating with students to define and solve complex problems without precedent, contributing to feedback and assessment, and helping students develop both the skills and mindsets to succeed in their studies and to flourish in their lives and careers beyond university.

The scale and impact of pre-planned technician-led teaching was evident in the timetable and in the quality of work presented for assessment, but remained much less visible during periods of self-directed study, when students sought personalised advice and guidance at the point of need, sometimes seeking assistance to realise an idea, or having reached the limits of their knowledge, or wanting to understand why something in their work had failed or resulted in an unanticipated outcome. Anecdotally, and through formal feedback channels, students consistently reported these unstructured exchanges with technicians as being among the most valuable and impactful pedagogies they experienced, both in terms of the quality of their outputs and in their confidence and abilities to enter their chosen careers.

The workforce, it seemed, was changing. Academic roles were becoming increasingly focused on theory, research, and curriculum development, while technicians took on more responsibility for teaching practical skills. In this new model, technicians increasingly found themselves positioned as the new ‘master practitioners’ holding specialist knowledge and occupying the pedagogic spaces their lecturer colleagues had previously held.

From my position within the university executive, I saw this change driven by role creep rather than strategy, and neither the operating model that funded it nor the structures or policies used to describe, manage, and quality-assure it kept pace. Furthermore, despite the clearly transformed roles and responsibilities, it remained problematic for technicians to claim that they teach.

My new book, Technical Teaching in Higher Education: Insights from the Creative Arts, examines and attempts to make sense of this shift, exploring the rich and textured pedagogies involved, and considering how institutions might use that understanding to improve teaching and learning.

Making sense of the technical turn

In my research, I describe the growing educational responsibilities of technicians as a ‘technical turn’. Within creative arts HE, I attribute this evolution to a combination of political, economic, social, and technological factors shaping the sector, accentuated by the incorporation and mergers of art schools and former polytechnics into universities.

Susan Orr theorises this shift in arts education as an ‘academic turn’ in which institutional missions and the hierarchies of knowledge taught and learned changed. Previously essential practical, tacit, and technical knowledge and skills became deprioritised in the curriculum, even as they remained central to student learning, experiences, and graduate outcomes. Jonathan Harwood’s concept of ‘academic drift’ offers a way of understanding these changes, which some critics associate with the loss of the traditional art school.

But neither the technical nor the academic turns, nor the role convergences they have enabled, are new or restricted to the creative arts. In 1997, the National Committee of Inquiry into Higher Education identified how the formerly clear distinctions between academic and non-academic roles were becoming increasingly blurred across the sector.

More recently, the UKRI-funded TALENT Commission on which I served provided evidence of the extent of technical involvement in teaching. Its national survey found that 95% of creative arts respondents were involved in teaching activities, compared with 75% of respondents from other disciplines. Subsequent studies have illuminated the scale and breadth of technician teaching across UK universities. These findings show that technical teaching extends across the sector, although how technicians understand and approach this work remains comparatively under-examined.

Five conceptions of technical teaching

My doctoral research addressed a related question: how do visual arts technicians understand and approach their teaching? Using phenomenography, I explored variation in participants’ conceptions of their pedagogies. I interviewed technicians across the UK in different kinds of institutions, spanning art, craft, design, and media disciplines. I examined what participants believed they taught, how they taught it, and why. I identified five approaches: Demonstrator, Instructor, Consultant, Collaborator, and Transformer. Each describes a different way of understanding and approaching teaching, and participants drew on several of these approaches depending on the learner and the context.

Demonstrators see their role as introducing learners to safe and competent practice. Their teaching makes equipment, materials, software, and specialist environments accessible through clear explanations and repeatable processes. They use didactic methods, while prioritising the clear understanding of foundations and conventions from which students can begin to work independently.

Instructors help students acquire, develop and apply skills in unique and personalised ways. Their emphasis moves towards adapting techniques to different purposes and developing the practical judgement needed to use them. Learning how to operate a camera, for example, becomes less about controls and functions, and more about understanding how its use can serve a photographic intention.

Consultants see themselves as subject authorities, whose role is to respond to a learner’s particular problem or ambition. A student may arrive with an unsuccessful process, a technical problem, or an idea they cannot realise. Teaching involves diagnostic assessment, questioning, and advice that help the learner evaluate possible solutions, evaluate risks and benefits, and make informed decisions.

Collaborators work alongside students, sharing in their processes of exploration and discovery. Knowledge develops through dialogue, experimentation, iteration, and encounters with materials or processes. These interactions and exchanges can take both student and technician beyond their existing understanding, supporting unknown and uncertain outcomes.

Transformers focus on changes in how learners understand their practice and themselves as practitioners. Their aim is to challenge and expand what students believe they can do, how they approach their work, and to broaden their ambitions and move beyond perceived limits. Transformative pedagogies were also found to influence curricula, more effectively integrate with academia, and inform institutional approaches to practical learning.

These five qualitatively distinct conceptions span a spectrum from teacher-centred content delivery to student-centred, transformative learning. They describe ways of understanding technical teaching, and an individual may adopt different pedagogies at different times. The range was broadly comparable with that identified in research on academics’ conceptions of teaching.

Putting the framework to use

The taxonomy’s practical value lies in making these different educational approaches and purposes more explicit. For individual technicians and their managers, it can provide language to reflect on practice, discuss teaching with peers, and identify development needs. It can also help educational developers connect teaching qualifications, mentoring, and professional recognition, such as Advance HE Fellowships, using authentic technical teaching and learning scenarios and case studies.

For curriculum teams, the framework can help identify where technical learning can be deployed most effectively within a programme and aligned with learning outcomes and assessment criteria. An equipment induction may prepare students to enter a workshop, but subsequent projects may depend on consultation, experimentation, and feedback.

Quality assurance and enhancement follow the same logic. Peer observation, student feedback, and shared reflection could help teams understand how technical pedagogies contribute to learning and where they need improvement.

For senior leaders, a clearer understanding of who teaches the curriculum and how is essential to linking strategy and operations. The academic/technical polarisation of the workforce is becoming increasingly unsustainable, prompting legitimate but challenging questions about workload planning, staffing structures and cost, and curriculum development. Such debates are likely to become more urgent as universities increasingly describe technician pedagogies as evidence of institutional teaching excellence, prioritise technical expertise and skills teaching, and place both at the centre of graduate outcomes and employability agendas.

The framework offers an evidence-based starting point for these conversations at a sector level; for institutions, it can help improve the integration of academic theory and technical practice within a constructively aligned curriculum, strengthen collaboration and understanding across role boundaries and break down longstanding silos in support of student education, experiences, and outcomes.

Dr Tim Savage is a consultant, author, and trainer specialising in technical learning, technicians, and institutional change in higher education. He previously served as Director of Technical Learning at the University for the Creative Arts and is a Principal Fellow of Advance HE, recognised for sustained strategic leadership in technical learning and teaching. His latest book, based on his doctoral research, is Technical Teaching in Higher Education: Insights from the Creative Arts (Routledge, 2026)

title: AI a scuola: cosa delegare senza perdere l’autonomia di pensiero
summary:
L’AI può migliorare i compiti senza aumentare l’apprendimento. Per scuole e università diventa decisivo stabilire quali attività delegare e in quali fasi dello studio, preservando le competenze necessarie a ragionare autonomamente e valutare le risposte delle macchine

L'articolo AI a scuola: cosa delegare senza perdere l’autonomia di pensiero proviene da Agenda Digitale.
full_text:
L’intelligenza artificiale è ormai entrata nello studio quotidiano molto più velocemente di quanto scuole e università siano riuscite a elaborarne le conseguenze. Le ricerche disponibili mostrano livelli di utilizzo ormai molto elevati tra gli studenti universitari e, soprattutto, un passaggio dall’uso occasionale alla presenza ordinaria dell’AI nelle attività di apprendimento. Una ricerca condotta in un college statunitense ha rilevato che, a meno di due anni dal lancio di ChatGPT, oltre l’80% degli studenti intervistati utilizzava già strumenti di intelligenza artificiale per finalità accademiche, sia per ottenere spiegazioni e feedback sia per automatizzare parti del lavoro richiesto (Contractor, Z. & Reyes, G., Generative AI in Higher Education: Evidence from an Elite College, 2025). Il dato interessante, tuttavia, non riguarda più soltanto quanti studenti utilizzino l’AI, ma quale parte del processo cognitivo stiano progressivamente affidandole.

Delega cognitiva e intelligenza artificiale: che cosa cambia nello studio

Riassumere un testo, cercare informazioni, predisporre una bibliografia, tradurre, correggere, organizzare appunti, costruire la struttura di un elaborato, formulare un’ipotesi, produrre domande di autovalutazione o spiegare un concetto difficile sono attività che fino a pochissimo tempo fa richiedevano direttamente l’intervento dello studente e che oggi possono essere svolte, almeno in parte, da un sistema generativo. L’OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026 introduce su questo punto una distinzione fondamentale: l’utilizzo dell’intelligenza artificiale può migliorare significativamente la capacità di svolgere un compito senza determinare necessariamente un corrispondente incremento dell’apprendimento.

Se l’AI viene utilizzata senza una progettazione pedagogica adeguata, avverte l’OCSE, l’esternalizzazione del lavoro può produrre migliori performance senza reali learning gains (OECD, Digital Education Outlook 2026: Exploring Effective Uses of Generative AI in Education, OECD Publishing, 2026). Possiamo quindi diventare più bravi a produrre risultati mentre diventiamo meno allenati a costruire i processi cognitivi necessari per raggiungerli autonomamente.

È qui che il digital learning incontra un concetto studiato da tempo dalle scienze cognitive, quello di cognitive offloading, l’esternalizzazione di alcune funzioni mentali verso strumenti presenti nell’ambiente. Non è un fenomeno nato con ChatGPT e non deve essere interpretato necessariamente in termini negativi. La scrittura stessa rappresenta una gigantesca tecnologia di esternalizzazione della memoria; una rubrica telefonica ci evita di ricordare centinaia di numeri; la calcolatrice trasferisce alla macchina alcune operazioni; i motori di ricerca hanno modificato il rapporto tra memoria e reperimento dell’informazione. La storia dell’intelligenza umana è anche la storia degli strumenti attraverso i quali abbiamo progressivamente trasferito all’esterno alcune attività cognitive per liberare risorse destinate ad attività più complesse.

Con l’intelligenza artificiale generativa, tuttavia, accade qualcosa di differente. Per la prima volta non stiamo delegando soltanto la conservazione dell’informazione o l’esecuzione di un calcolo, ma funzioni che si collocano molto più vicino al cuore del ragionamento: sintetizzare, argomentare, confrontare, classificare, formulare ipotesi, individuare connessioni. Non stiamo semplicemente esternalizzando la memoria. Stiamo iniziando a esternalizzare parti del processo attraverso il quale attribuiamo forma al pensiero. È proprio questa differenza a rendere insufficiente la tradizionale contrapposizione tra favorevoli e contrari all’AI nella scuola.

AI e apprendimento: il confine tra supporto e sostituzione

La domanda educativa corretta, infatti, non può essere se sia giusto o sbagliato delegare. L’essere umano ha sempre costruito il proprio progresso attraverso la delega tecnologica. La domanda diventa piuttosto che cosa possiamo permetterci di delegare senza perdere le capacità necessarie per controllare ciò che abbiamo delegato. Uno studente che utilizza l’intelligenza artificiale per ottenere una sintesi dopo avere letto e compreso un documento compie un’operazione completamente diversa da chi utilizza quella stessa sintesi per evitare di confrontarsi con il testo originale. Nel primo caso la tecnologia comprime un’attività; nel secondo rischia di eliminare l’esperienza cognitiva attraverso cui quella competenza avrebbe dovuto formarsi.

Le prime evidenze sperimentali invitano proprio a osservare questa distinzione con attenzione. Alcuni studi recenti rilevano una riduzione dell’impegno cognitivo quando l’AI viene utilizzata per svolgere attività di scrittura e problem solving, mentre altre ricerche mostrano che un utilizzo pedagogicamente guidato può produrre effetti positivi. Non siamo quindi davanti a una tecnologia intrinsecamente capace di impoverire o potenziare l’apprendimento. La stessa intelligenza artificiale può diventare una protesi che amplifica il pensiero oppure una scorciatoia che evita di esercitarlo. È il modo in cui viene inserita nel processo educativo a determinare la differenza.

Ed è probabilmente proprio qui che si apre la grande questione che scuole e università dovranno affrontare nei prossimi anni. Finora abbiamo cercato soprattutto di insegnare agli studenti come utilizzare l’intelligenza artificiale. Forse dobbiamo cominciare a insegnare qualcosa di più difficile: quando utilizzarla, quando limitarla e, soprattutto, quando scegliere consapevolmente di pensare senza di essa.

La soglia di delega cognitiva nell’uso dell’AI

Se il problema non è più stabilire se utilizzare l’intelligenza artificiale, ma comprendere quali funzioni cognitive possiamo affidarle senza impoverire quelle umane, allora la scuola dovrà probabilmente introdurre un principio nuovo: quello della soglia di delega cognitiva. Non tutte le attività che una macchina può svolgere al nostro posto devono necessariamente essere delegate, soprattutto durante il periodo nel quale una competenza si sta formando. Un adulto che utilizza un navigatore dopo avere sviluppato capacità di orientamento compie un’operazione diversa da un bambino che cresce senza esercitarle mai; allo stesso modo, uno studente capace di argomentare può utilizzare l’AI per confrontare e migliorare le proprie tesi, mentre chi affida immediatamente al sistema la costruzione dell’argomentazione rischia di ottenere un prodotto formalmente migliore senza avere sviluppato la competenza che quel prodotto dovrebbe dimostrare. La questione educativa non è quindi quanto sia potente l’AI, ma in quale momento del processo di apprendimento sia pedagogicamente utile permetterle di diventarlo.

Delega sostitutiva e delega aumentativa

Le evidenze più recenti suggeriscono proprio la necessità di distinguere tra delega sostitutiva e delega aumentativa. Alcuni studi mostrano che un utilizzo non guidato della GenAI può favorire superficialità nell’elaborazione, minore autoregolazione dello sforzo e dipendenza dal supporto artificiale, mentre altre sperimentazioni evidenziano risultati differenti quando il sistema viene progettato per porre domande, offrire feedback progressivi e costringere lo studente a esplicitare il proprio ragionamento. Uno studio pubblicato sul British Journal of Educational Technology ha definito significativamente questo rischio attraverso il concetto di metacognitive laziness, mostrando come il supporto generativo possa migliorare alcuni risultati immediati e contemporaneamente ridurre motivazione e coinvolgimento nei processi metacognitivi quando lo studente trasferisce alla macchina una parte eccessiva della regolazione del proprio apprendimento (Fan et al., Beware of metacognitive laziness: Effects of generative artificial intelligence on learning motivation, processes, and performance, British Journal of Educational Technology, https://doi.org/10.1111/bjet.13544). Il problema, quindi, non sembra essere semplicemente la presenza dell’AI, ma il tipo di relazione cognitiva che costruiamo con essa.

Progettare diversi livelli di autonomia cognitiva

Da questa prospettiva potrebbe emergere una nuova funzione della progettazione didattica. Non dovremmo più limitarci a distinguere attività nelle quali l’intelligenza artificiale è consentita da quelle nelle quali è vietata, una separazione destinata probabilmente a diventare sempre meno sostenibile, ma progettare diversi livelli di autonomia cognitiva. In alcune fasi lo studente dovrebbe ragionare senza supporto artificiale, perché è necessario consolidare conoscenze, memoria, capacità argomentativa e problem solving; in altre potrebbe confrontare il proprio risultato con quello prodotto dall’AI, individuandone differenze ed errori; in altre ancora potrebbe utilizzarla liberamente per esplorare alternative, simulare scenari e raggiungere risultati che individualmente non sarebbe in grado di ottenere. L’obiettivo non sarebbe proteggere artificialmente una mente “pura” dalla tecnologia, ma costruire la capacità di scegliere consapevolmente quale intelligenza utilizzare in ogni situazione.

È una prospettiva coerente con l’AI Competency Framework for Students dell’UNESCO, che non riduce l’alfabetizzazione all’intelligenza artificiale alla capacità tecnica di utilizzare strumenti, ma la organizza attorno a una mentalità human-centred, all’etica dell’AI, alla comprensione delle tecniche e delle applicazioni e alla progettazione dei sistemi, articolando le competenze nei livelli comprendere, applicare e creare (UNESCO, AI competency framework for students, 2024). Essere competenti nell’uso dell’AI significa quindi anche conservare la capacità di giudicarla, riconoscendo quando una risposta apparentemente convincente è fragile, quando un’automazione riduce invece di ampliare le nostre possibilità e quando la delega diventa dipendenza. (UNESCO)

Metacognizione aumentata: riconoscere ciò che deleghiamo all’AI

Questo passaggio modifica profondamente anche il significato della metacognizione. Se fino a ieri significava soprattutto essere consapevoli di come apprendiamo, domani dovrà comprendere anche la capacità di riconoscere quali parti del nostro processo cognitivo stiamo trasferendo all’esterno. Lo studente dovrebbe imparare a domandarsi non soltanto se la risposta ottenuta dall’AI sia corretta, ma quale operazione mentale avrebbe dovuto compiere per produrla, se possiede ancora quella capacità e se delegarla in quella particolare circostanza rappresenti un vantaggio oppure una rinuncia. È una forma di consapevolezza completamente nuova, che potremmo definire metacognizione aumentata: conoscere il funzionamento della propria mente significa anche conoscere i confini continuamente mobili tra ciò che facciamo noi e ciò che lasciamo fare alle nostre estensioni artificiali.

La posta in gioco, del resto, supera ampiamente la scuola. Una generazione abituata a delegare sistematicamente sintesi, interpretazione, decisione e argomentazione porterà queste abitudini cognitive nell’università, nel lavoro e nella vita democratica. L’UNESCO ha recentemente richiamato proprio il rapporto tra autonomia dell’AI e agency umana: aumentando l’autonomia affidata ai sistemi artificiali, occorre progettare deliberatamente condizioni capaci di preservare quella delle persone (UNESCO, AI operators or creators? Two visions of agency and learning)

Educazione e AI: imparare anche quando non usarla

Forse, allora, dovremo abbandonare l’idea che l’obiettivo dell’educazione nell’era dell’AI sia semplicemente insegnare a utilizzare bene strumenti sempre più potenti. La missione potrebbe essere molto più ambiziosa: insegnare a costruire un equilibrio consapevole tra capacità proprie e capacità delegate, sapendo che la frontiera continuerà inevitabilmente a spostarsi. La calcolatrice ci ha permesso di delegare il calcolo senza eliminare la matematica; Internet ci ha consentito di delegare parte della memoria senza rendere inutile la conoscenza. L’intelligenza artificiale ci permetterà probabilmente di delegare una parte molto più ampia del lavoro cognitivo, ma proprio per questo dovremo decidere quali capacità continuare intenzionalmente a esercitare.

Metacognizione aumentata: riconoscere ciò che deleghiamo all’AI

Questo passaggio modifica profondamente anche il significato della metacognizione. Se fino a ieri significava soprattutto essere consapevoli di come apprendiamo, domani dovrà comprendere anche la capacità di riconoscere quali parti del nostro processo cognitivo stiamo trasferendo all’esterno. Lo studente dovrebbe imparare a domandarsi non soltanto se la risposta ottenuta dall’AI sia corretta, ma quale operazione mentale avrebbe dovuto compiere per produrla, se possiede ancora quella capacità e se delegarla in quella particolare circostanza rappresenti un vantaggio oppure una rinuncia. È una forma di consapevolezza completamente nuova, che potremmo definire metacognizione aumentata: conoscere il funzionamento della propria mente significa anche conoscere i confini continuamente mobili tra ciò che facciamo noi e ciò che lasciamo fare alle nostre estensioni artificiali.

La posta in gioco, del resto, supera ampiamente la scuola. Una generazione abituata a delegare sistematicamente sintesi, interpretazione, decisione e argomentazione porterà queste abitudini cognitive nell’università, nel lavoro e nella vita democratica. L’UNESCO ha recentemente richiamato proprio il rapporto tra autonomia dell’AI e agency umana: aumentando l’autonomia affidata ai sistemi artificiali, occorre progettare deliberatamente condizioni capaci di preservare quella delle persone (UNESCO, AI operators or creators? Two visions of agency and learning)

Educazione e AI: imparare anche quando non usarla

Forse, allora, dovremo abbandonare l’idea che l’obiettivo dell’educazione nell’era dell’AI sia semplicemente insegnare a utilizzare bene strumenti sempre più potenti. La missione potrebbe essere molto più ambiziosa: insegnare a costruire un equilibrio consapevole tra capacità proprie e capacità delegate, sapendo che la frontiera continuerà inevitabilmente a spostarsi. La calcolatrice ci ha permesso di delegare il calcolo senza eliminare la matematica; Internet ci ha consentito di delegare parte della memoria senza rendere inutile la conoscenza. L’intelligenza artificiale ci permetterà probabilmente di delegare una parte molto più ampia del lavoro cognitivo, ma proprio per questo dovremo decidere quali capacità continuare intenzionalmente a esercitare.
